sceneHappening: Ananias and Sapphira, arrest and rescue, and Gamaliel's advice
summary: A man named Ananias, with his wife Sapphira, sells a possession and, with his wife's knowledge, keeps back part of the price, and brings a part and lays it at the apostles' feet. Peter says, "Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and to keep back part of the price of the land? While it remained, did it not remain yours? After it was sold, wasn't it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven't lied to men, but to God." Hearing these words, Ananias falls down and dies, and great fear comes on all who hear it. About three hours later his wife comes in, not knowing what has happened. Peter asks, "Tell me whether you sold the land for so much," and she says yes. "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out." She falls down at once and dies. Great fear comes on the whole church. Many signs and wonders are done among the people by the apostles, who are all with one accord in Solomon's portico, and people bring the sick out into the streets and lay them on cots and mats, so that as Peter passes by, at least his shadow may fall on some of them. Crowds also gather from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people and those afflicted by unclean spirits, and they are all healed. The high priest and all those with him, the sect of the Sadducees, are filled with jealousy and arrest the apostles and put them in public custody, but an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors by night and brings them out: "Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life." They enter the temple about daybreak and teach. The council sends to the prison to have them brought, and the officers find the prison locked and the guards standing at the doors, but no one inside. Someone reports, "The men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching." The captain brings them without violence, for they fear the people. The high priest says, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, and behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man's blood on us." Peter and the apostles answer, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree. God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins. We are his witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him." They are furious and want to kill them. But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, respected by all the people, stands up and orders the men put outside for a little while: "Men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do. For before these days Theudas rose up, saying that he was somebody; a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves to him, who was slain, and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed and came to nothing. After him, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad. Now I tell you, refrain from these men, and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown. But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you might even be found fighting against God." They agree with him, and when they have called in the apostles, they beat them and charge them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go. The apostles depart from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the Name. Every day, in the temple and at home, they do not stop teaching and preaching Jesus as the Christ.
whySettingMatters: Ananias and Sapphira's sin is not keeping money back, since Peter says the land was theirs to keep, but lying about it, to appear more generous than they were; the account is meant to show the seriousness of deceit in a community founded on trust, and a contrast with Barnabas in 4:36-37. The word "church" (ekklēsia) appears for the first time in Acts here (5:11). The parallel with Achan in Joshua 7 is often drawn. People laying the sick in the street, hoping Peter's shadow would fall on them, is told without comment on whether it worked or whether Peter approved. The Sadducees are the priestly party who had the most to lose from a movement preaching resurrection. The angel opening the prison doors is the first of three prison escapes in Acts (see 12:6-11 and 16:25-34). The apostles' answer, "We must obey God rather than men," is the core of the story. Gamaliel was a leading Pharisee and the teacher of Saul (22:3); his advice is practical and prudent. His mention of Theudas and of Judas of Galilee raises a historical puzzle, since Josephus places a Theudas around AD 44-46, later than Gamaliel's speech; whether Luke has made an error, or there were two men by that name, is debated. Beating the apostles was the whipping of thirty-nine lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), and they rejoice that they are counted worthy to suffer for the name.

questions: Ananias and Sapphira lied about their gift. Why does Luke place this scene right after Barnabas?
Peter says, "We must obey God rather than men." What are the limits of that, as the apostles live it?
Gamaliel says, "If it is of God, you cannot overthrow it." Is that a safe test, and what does it assume?
The apostles rejoice at being beaten. How is that different from what you would expect?
